name: frg (fastripgrep)
workload: 8 regex/literal/alternation/wildcard patterns searched over the openclaw codebase (9,000 files), case-sensitive, warm cache, output to /dev/null, comparing frg's sparse n-gram index against ripgrep and grep.
claimed_speedup: 5.3x faster than ripgrep on a selective literal search (10ms vs 53ms); wins on all 8 tested pattern types vs ripgrep (1.06x-5.3x); up to ~150x faster than grep on the same literal pattern (1553ms vs 10ms); 100% match-count parity with ripgrep
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release; no rustc version or CPU-specific flags stated
tradeoffs: Requires an upfront index build (~20-23s for 9K files; incremental updates ~70ms via overlay/tombstone); index must be kept in sync (frg update/watch); adds a .frg/ directory to the repo tree; falls back to brute-force scan for patterns with no extractable literals.
caveats: First-party README benchmark only. CPU model and Rust toolchain version are not stated, so despite public bench code (benches/bench.rs) this falls short of tier A. Not stated how many repeats each row reflects.

name: Tantivy
workload: English Wikipedia corpus; queries derived from the AOL query dataset (2+ terms, >=1 phrase hit) run as intersection/union/phrase queries under COUNT / TOP-10 BM25 / TOP-10+COUNT collectors; single-threaded, best-of-N runs, warm page cache and JIT.
claimed_speedup: approximately 2x faster search latency than Lucene (project's own summary of the multi-query benchmark suite)
compiler_and_flags: Rust 1.96.0 (release build via the benchmark's Makefile) for Tantivy; OpenJDK 21.0.11 for Lucene
stars_or_usage: 16.1k stars; used in production by Etsy, ParadeDB, Nuclia, Element.io, and others
tradeoffs: Immutable segments (documents must be deleted and reindexed to edit); library, not a standalone server (Quickwit is the distributed-search layer built on top); Rust-only core API (bindings exist for Python/Ruby).
caveats: The '~2x' figure is the project's own summary of a benchmark suite (github.com/quickwit-oss/search-benchmark-game) with many per-query-type results (intersection/union/phrase x COUNT/TOP-10 combos) that vary by test, not a single universal ratio. The live results dashboard (tantivy-search.github.io/bench/) is JS-rendered and could not be scraped for exact per-query numbers this session; the benchmark repo's stated methodology, hardware, and toolchain versions were verified directly instead.

name: IResearch (SereneDB)
workload: Same Search Benchmark Game suite used for the Tantivy-vs-Lucene comparison: English Wikipedia corpus, AOL-derived multi-term queries run as intersection/union/phrase queries under COUNT / TOP-10 BM25 / TOP-10+COUNT collectors, single-threaded, best-of-N runs, warm page cache.
claimed_speedup: up to 5x faster than Lucene and Tantivy on the Search Benchmark Game; results were reviewed and merged into the benchmark repo by the Tantivy maintainers themselves (commit f4149454e8de6d97a0b5c1b4253db1a6e2c82622, engine id iresearch-26.03.1)
compiler_and_flags: Built via the search-benchmark-game harness alongside Rust 1.96.0 (Tantivy) / OpenJDK 21.0.11 (Lucene); the exact C++ compiler/flags used for IResearch's own build are not separately itemized in the repo beyond the shared Makefile.
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, Manjaro Linux (rolling), kernel 7.0.3-1-MANJARO (same benchmark host as the Tantivy vs. Lucene run in this suite)
stars_or_usage: 831 stars (serenedb/serenedb monorepo); production search backend since 2018 (originally ArangoSearch)
tradeoffs: C++ library embedded via CMake (target iresearch-static), not a standalone server; JVM-free; the 5x headline also includes beating Tantivy, which is not one of this category's three named baselines (only the Lucene comparison counts here).
caveats: Originally developed at iresearch-toolkit/iresearch (now archived) and moved into serenedb/serenedb as the iresearch/ subdirectory; is_fork_of left null since this is a repository migration by the same maintainers, not a third-party fork. The '5x' headline is IResearch's own framing of results it contributed to a third-party-hosted benchmark suite whose maintainers reviewed and merged the change (stronger than a pure self-benchmark, but still vendor-initiated); per-query results vary and are not individually broken out here.

name: ngi (N-gram Indexed Regex Search)
workload: 5 regex patterns (attribute macros, function calls, struct names, exported symbols, mutex usage) searched across the Linux kernel source tree (92,916 files) using ngi's trigram index + ripgrep verification, compared against plain ripgrep and grep -r.
claimed_speedup: 1.7x-5.9x faster than ripgrep and 13x-69x faster than grep across the 5 tested patterns on the Linux kernel (e.g. 27ms vs rg's 161ms vs grep's 1866ms for `__attribute__.*section`); 100% match parity with ripgrep (13/13 test queries)
compiler_and_flags: cargo build --release; no CPU model or rustc version stated
tradeoffs: Falls back to a full ripgrep scan when more than ~10% of files match a query (index only helps selective queries); index build takes ~16s for the Linux kernel and produces a 146MB index that must be kept current; depends on ripgrep being on PATH for best performance (falls back to a built-in Rust regex engine otherwise).
caveats: First-party README benchmark on a fixed, named corpus (Linux kernel) with a reproducible pattern list, but hardware/CPU model and exact toolchain version are not stated, so it falls short of tier A.

name: trigrep
workload: Search-only benchmark on a clone of git/git (patterns: TODO|FIXME, ^#include, struct [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*, parse), 5 timed runs + 1 warmup per pattern per tool, trigram index pre-built before timing (make benchmark).
claimed_speedup: ~1.58x faster than ripgrep and ~14.79x faster than grep by mean query time (0.0405s trigrep vs 0.0640s ripgrep vs 0.5990s grep)
compiler_and_flags: Built via `make build`/cargo; no rustc version or optimization flags stated
tradeoffs: Requires an explicit `trigrep index .` step before searching; no license file present, so the code can be studied but not legally reused/redistributed.
caveats: No OSI license in the repo (usability=reference, not copyable). Benchmark methodology is unusually well documented for a first-party result (pinned source commit, timestamp, run/warmup counts all recorded), but CPU model is still not stated, capping it at tier C.
